header:
How McDonald's became
a real estate empire

lines.text: McDonald's made more from rent than from selling its own food.
lines.say: McDonald's made more from rent than from selling its own food.

lines.text: In 2025, franchisees paid McDonald's $10.4 billion in rent. Its own restaurants sold $9.7 billion of food.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, franchisees paid McDonald's ten point four billion dollars in rent. Its own restaurants sold nine point seven billion dollars of food.

lines.text: Rent won by $752 million. The world's best-known burger chain is also a giant landlord.
lines.say: Rent won by about seven hundred fifty million dollars. The world's best-known burger chain is also a giant landlord.

lines.text: And in September 2026, that landlord offered its tenants rent relief, as part of an $8.5 billion plan.
lines.say: And in September twenty twenty-six, that landlord offered its tenants rent relief, as part of an eight point five billion dollar plan.

lines.text: So how did a burger chain become a landlord? The history, the money, the rent math, and the risks.
lines.say: So how did a burger chain become a landlord? We'll cover the history, the money, the rent math, and the risks.

lines.text: No stock tips here. Just how the machine makes money.
lines.say: No stock tips here. Just how the machine makes money.

lines.text: Chapter 1: The landlord idea.
lines.say: Chapter one: the landlord idea.

lines.text: In 1955, a milkshake-mixer salesman named Ray Kroc opened his first McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois.
lines.say: In nineteen fifty-five, a milkshake-mixer salesman named Ray Kroc opened his first McDonald's, in Des Plaines, Illinois.

lines.text: He'd struck a deal with the McDonald brothers to sell franchises of their fast, simple burger system.
lines.say: He'd struck a deal with the McDonald brothers to sell franchises of their fast, simple burger system.

lines.text: Franchisees paid 1.9% of sales. Half a point went to the McDonald brothers, so Kroc kept 1.4%.
lines.say: Franchisees paid one point nine percent of their sales. Half a point of that went to the McDonald brothers, so Kroc kept one point four percent.

lines.text: On a 15-cent hamburger, 1.4% is about a fifth of a cent. That's not an empire.
lines.say: On a fifteen-cent hamburger, one point four percent is about a fifth of a cent. That's not an empire.

lines.text: Then, in 1956, a finance executive named Harry Sonneborn joined Kroc with a different idea: control the ground under the restaurants.
lines.say: Then, in nineteen fifty-six, a finance executive named Harry Sonneborn joined Kroc with a different idea: control the ground under the restaurants.

lines.text: They set up a separate company, Franchise Realty Corporation, to lease or buy restaurant sites.
lines.say: They set up a separate company, Franchise Realty Corporation, to lease or buy restaurant sites.

lines.text: The playbook: find a good corner, then lease or buy the land.
lines.say: The playbook went like this. Find a good corner, then lease or buy the land.

lines.text: Build the restaurant, then rent the whole package to the franchisee, at a markup or a share of sales, whichever was bigger.
lines.say: Build the restaurant, then rent the whole package to the franchisee, at a markup or a share of sales, whichever was bigger.

lines.text: From then on, the money flowed two ways: a small cut of sales as a fee, and a much bigger check as rent.
lines.say: From then on, the money flowed two ways: a small cut of sales as a fee, and a much bigger check as rent.

lines.text: It also gave McDonald's control. The franchisee's license and lease came as one package.
lines.say: It also gave McDonald's control. The franchisee's license and the lease came as one package.

lines.text: And it worked. McDonald's went from 31 restaurants at the end of 1957 to 228 by 1960.
lines.say: And it worked. McDonald's went from thirty-one restaurants at the end of nineteen fifty-seven to two hundred twenty-eight by nineteen sixty.

lines.text: In 1961, Kroc bought out the McDonald brothers for $2.7 million.
lines.say: In nineteen sixty-one, Kroc bought out the McDonald brothers for two point seven million dollars.

lines.text: Sonneborn went on to run the company as its president from 1959 to 1967.
lines.say: Sonneborn went on to run the company as its president, from nineteen fifty-nine to nineteen sixty-seven.

lines.text: "We are not technically in the food business. We are in the real estate business." Harry Sonneborn, as quoted in John Love's 1986 company history.
lines.say: In John Love's nineteen eighty-six company history, Sonneborn is quoted telling investors: We are not technically in the food business. We are in the real estate business.

scene.text: We are not technically in the food business. We are in the real estate business.

lines.text: His point: the hamburgers are how the tenants pay the rent.
lines.say: His point was simple: the hamburgers are how the tenants pay the rent.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Follow the money.
lines.say: Chapter two: follow the money.

lines.text: Fast forward to 2025. McDonald's had 45,356 restaurants worldwide, and about 95% were run by franchisees.
lines.say: Fast forward to twenty twenty-five. McDonald's had forty-five thousand three hundred fifty-six restaurants worldwide, and about ninety-five percent were run by franchisees.

lines.text: Together they rang up more than $139 billion in sales in 2025. But most of that money belongs to the franchisees.
lines.say: Together, they rang up more than one hundred thirty-nine billion dollars in sales in twenty twenty-five. But most of that money belongs to the franchisees, not to McDonald's.

lines.text: McDonald's own revenue was $26.9 billion. It came from three big buckets, plus a small one.
lines.say: McDonald's own revenue was twenty-six point nine billion dollars. It came from three big buckets, plus a small one.

lines.text: Bucket one: rent from franchisees, $10.4 billion.
lines.say: Bucket one is rent from franchisees: ten point four billion dollars.

lines.text: Bucket two: royalties, a cut of every franchisee's sales, $6.0 billion.
lines.say: Bucket two is royalties, a cut of every franchisee's sales: six billion dollars.

lines.text: Bucket three: food sold at its own restaurants, $9.7 billion. Plus $647 million of other revenue.
lines.say: Bucket three is food sold at its own restaurants: nine point seven billion. Plus six hundred forty-seven million dollars of other revenue.

lines.text: Initial fees, paid when a franchisee opens or takes over a restaurant, were tiny by comparison: $88 million.
lines.say: Initial fees, paid when a franchisee opens or takes over a restaurant, were tiny by comparison: just eighty-eight million dollars.

lines.text: Add rent, royalties and small initial fees, and franchisees sent McDonald's $16,548 million in 2025.
lines.say: Add up rent, royalties and small initial fees, and franchisees sent McDonald's about sixteen and a half billion dollars in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That's about 62% of all its revenue. And inside that franchise money, rent was 63.1% and royalties 36.4%.
lines.say: That's about sixty-two percent of all its revenue. And inside that franchise money, rent was about sixty-three percent, and royalties about thirty-six.

lines.text: That's $1.74 of rent for every $1 of royalties. The landlord part is the bigger part.
lines.say: That's a dollar seventy-four of rent for every dollar of royalties. The landlord part is the bigger part.

lines.text: And the rent has kept climbing: from $7.5 billion in 2019 to $10.4 billion in 2025.
lines.say: And the rent has kept climbing: from seven point five billion dollars in twenty nineteen to ten point four billion in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: The one dip was 2020, when the pandemic hit sales and rent fell to $6.8 billion.
lines.say: The one dip was twenty twenty, when the pandemic hit sales and rent fell to six point eight billion.

lines.text: From 2019 to 2025, rent rose about 39%.
lines.say: From twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-five, rent rose about thirty-nine percent.

lines.text: Why does it climb? The rent is based on a percent of sales, with a minimum. When franchisees sell more, the landlord collects more.
lines.say: Why does it climb? The rent is based on a percent of sales, with a minimum. When franchisees sell more, the landlord collects more.

lines.text: That held into 2026. In the April-to-June quarter, franchised revenues rose 4%, to $4.39 billion.
lines.say: That held into twenty twenty-six. In the April-to-June quarter, franchised revenues rose four percent, to four point three nine billion dollars.

lines.text: And franchised margins, what's left after McDonald's own property costs, rose 4.3% to about $3.71 billion in that quarter.
lines.say: And franchised margins, what's left after McDonald's own property costs, rose four point three percent, to about three point seven one billion dollars in that quarter.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The rent math.
lines.say: Chapter three: the rent math.

lines.text: Let's run one hypothetical U.S. restaurant through the numbers. It's an example, not a real store.
lines.say: Let's run one hypothetical US restaurant through the numbers. It's an example, not a real store.

lines.text: Say it sells $4 million a year. The 2024 U.S. average for a traditional McDonald's was $4,002,000.
lines.say: Say it sells four million dollars a year. That's close to the twenty twenty-four US average for a traditional McDonald's, which was four million two thousand dollars.

lines.text: Since 2024, new U.S. restaurants pay a 5% royalty, up from 4%. 5% of $4 million is $200,000.
lines.say: Since twenty twenty-four, new US restaurants pay a five percent royalty, up from four. Five percent of four million is two hundred thousand dollars.

lines.text: Rent varies a lot by location. For this example, assume 10% of sales. That's another $400,000.
lines.say: Rent varies a lot by location. For this example, let's assume ten percent of sales. That's another four hundred thousand dollars.

lines.text: $200,000 + $400,000 = $600,000. That's 15% of sales going to McDonald's.
lines.say: Two hundred thousand plus four hundred thousand is six hundred thousand dollars. That's fifteen percent of sales going to McDonald's.

lines.text: That leaves $3.4 million for the franchisee to pay for food, paper, payroll, ads, equipment and loans.
lines.say: That leaves three point four million dollars for the franchisee to pay for food, paper, payroll, advertising, equipment and loans.

lines.text: Here's the clever part: the fee is based on sales, not profit.
lines.say: Here's the clever part. The fee is based on sales, not profit.

lines.text: If sales rise 10%, to $4.4 million, McDonald's collects $660,000. That's $60,000 more, whether or not the owner's profit rose.
lines.say: If sales rise ten percent, to four point four million, McDonald's collects six hundred sixty thousand dollars. That's sixty thousand more, whether or not the owner's profit rose.

lines.text: The split of jobs: McDonald's provides the land and building. The franchisee pays for equipment, signs and seating, and runs the place.
lines.say: Here's the split of jobs. McDonald's provides the land and the building. The franchisee pays for equipment, signs and seating, and runs the place.

lines.text: For McDonald's, that's a great trade. In 2025, it kept 84.2% of its franchise revenue as margin, after property costs.
lines.say: For McDonald's, that's a very good trade. In twenty twenty-five, it kept about eighty-four percent of its franchise revenue as margin, after property costs.

lines.text: On food sold at its own restaurants, after food, wages and rent-type costs, it kept just 14.7%.
lines.say: On food sold at its own restaurants, after paying for food, wages and occupancy, it kept just about fifteen percent.

lines.text: So franchised restaurants made about 90% of its restaurant margin dollars: $13.9 billion of $15.4 billion.
lines.say: So franchised restaurants made about ninety percent of its restaurant margin dollars: thirteen point nine billion out of fifteen point four billion.

lines.text: Selling burgers is a thin-margin business. Collecting rent and royalties is a thick one.
lines.say: Selling burgers is a thin-margin business. Collecting rent and royalties is a thick one.

lines.text: Chapter 4: What it owns.
lines.say: Chapter four: what it owns.

lines.text: So what's actually in the empire? At the end of 2025, McDonald's owned about 56% of the land and 80% of the buildings in its consolidated markets.
lines.say: So what's actually in the empire? At the end of twenty twenty-five, McDonald's owned about fifty-six percent of the land, and eighty percent of the buildings, for restaurants in its consolidated markets.

lines.text: Consolidated markets are the ones McDonald's runs directly, like the U.S. In licensed markets, local partners generally provide the real estate.
lines.say: Consolidated markets are the ones McDonald's runs directly, like the US. In developmental licensed markets, local partners generally provide the real estate.

lines.text: Where it doesn't own the land, it usually holds a long-term lease, then rents to the franchisee. Landlord either way.
lines.say: Where it doesn't own the land, it usually holds a long-term lease, then rents to the franchisee. It's the landlord either way.

lines.text: On its books, McDonald's property and equipment cost $49.3 billion, as of December 31, 2025.
lines.say: On its books, McDonald's property and equipment cost forty-nine point three billion dollars, as of the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Most of that is buildings, $37.7 billion, plus $8.2 billion of land.
lines.say: Most of that is buildings, thirty-seven point seven billion dollars, plus eight point two billion of land.

lines.text: Equipment and everything else adds about $3.4 billion more.
lines.say: Equipment and everything else adds about three point four billion more.

lines.text: Here's a twist: $15.5 billion of those buildings sit on land McDonald's leases. It rents the ground, builds on it, and rents it back out.
lines.say: Here's a twist. Fifteen point five billion dollars of those buildings sit on land McDonald's leases. It rents the ground, builds on it, and rents it back out.

lines.text: And that's at cost. Land bought decades ago sits on the books at old prices, not at what it would sell for.
lines.say: And that's at cost. Land bought decades ago sits on the books at old prices, not at what it would sell for.

lines.text: The deals are long, too. A typical franchise arrangement runs 20 years.
lines.say: The deals are long, too. A typical franchise arrangement runs twenty years.

lines.text: When it ends, McDonald's keeps control of the land and building. It can sign the same operator, pick a new one, or close the store.
lines.say: When it ends, McDonald's keeps control of the land and the building. It can sign the same operator again, pick a new one, or close the store.

lines.text: So the empire isn't really the burger recipe. It's tens of thousands of busy street corners.
lines.say: So the empire isn't really the burger recipe. It's tens of thousands of busy street corners.

lines.text: Chapter 5: The risks, and you.
lines.say: Chapter five: the risks, and you.

lines.text: But a landlord is only as strong as its tenants. If franchisees struggle, the rent model gets tested.
lines.say: But a landlord is only as strong as its tenants. If franchisees struggle, the rent model gets tested.

lines.text: And U.S. sales growth slowed in 2026. In the April-to-June quarter, U.S. comparable sales rose just 0.8%.
lines.say: And US sales growth slowed in twenty twenty-six. In the April-to-June quarter, US comparable sales rose just zero point eight percent.

lines.text: That's the backdrop for September 23, 2026, when McDonald's laid out about $8.5 billion of support for franchisees through 2036.
lines.say: That's the backdrop for September twenty-third, twenty twenty-six. At its investor day, McDonald's laid out about eight point five billion dollars of support for franchisees through twenty thirty-six.

lines.text: It's a mix of rent relief and capital support, with about $5 billion of it through 2030.
lines.say: It's a mix of rent relief and capital support, with about five billion dollars of it through twenty thirty.

lines.text: The goal: help pay for new equipment and tech that the company puts at about $800,000 per U.S. restaurant.
lines.say: The goal is to help pay for new equipment and technology that the company puts at about eight hundred thousand dollars per US restaurant.

lines.text: Notice what's happening: the landlord is easing up on rent so its tenants can afford to upgrade.
lines.say: Notice what's happening. The landlord is easing up on rent so its tenants can afford to upgrade.

lines.text: Owning the real estate is what gives McDonald's that lever. A royalty-only franchisor has no rent to cut.
lines.say: Owning the real estate is what gives McDonald's that lever. A franchisor that only collects royalties has no rent to cut.

lines.text: McDonald's estimates the upgrades add about $100,000 a year in cash flow for an average U.S. restaurant, paying back in about 4 years.
lines.say: McDonald's estimates the upgrades add about a hundred thousand dollars a year in cash flow for an average US restaurant, paying back in about four years.

lines.text: That's the company's own estimate, not a guarantee. Franchisees will find out store by store.
lines.say: That's the company's own estimate, not a guarantee. Franchisees will find out store by store.

lines.text: The system keeps growing, too: more than 46,000 restaurants by September 2026. McDonald's also targeted net restaurant growth of over 4.5% in 2027.
lines.say: The system keeps growing, too: more than forty-six thousand restaurants by September twenty twenty-six. McDonald's also targeted net restaurant growth of over four and a half percent in twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: For a landlord, every new restaurant is a new tenant, paying rent on its sales.
lines.say: For a landlord, every new restaurant is one more tenant, paying rent on its sales.

lines.text: Other risks: first, if store sales slow, percent-of-sales rent slows with them, down toward the minimums.
lines.say: There are other risks, too. First, if store sales slow, percent-of-sales rent slows with them, down toward the minimums.

lines.text: Second, fees on sales can squeeze operators. Trade press reports that on delivery orders, the app takes its cut, but rent and royalty still apply to the full sale.
lines.say: Second, fees on sales can squeeze operators. Trade press has reported that on delivery orders, the app takes its cut, but rent and royalty still apply to the full sale.

lines.text: Third, real estate isn't free. McDonald's pays its own leases, depreciation and upkeep, busy store or not.
lines.say: Third, real estate isn't free. McDonald's pays its own leases, depreciation and upkeep, busy store or not.

lines.text: So what does it mean for you at the counter? In our example, 15 cents of every dollar you spend goes to McDonald's as rent and royalty.
lines.say: So what does it mean for you at the counter? In our example, fifteen cents of every dollar you spend goes to McDonald's as rent and royalty.

lines.text: Because that take rides on sales, McDonald's collects more when the register rings more, from more visits or higher prices.
lines.say: Because that take rides on sales, McDonald's collects more whenever the register rings more, whether from more visits or from higher prices.

lines.text: Food and labor costs stay with the franchisee. So a deal that lifts sales but thins margins can help the landlord more than the operator.
lines.say: Food and labor costs stay with the franchisee. So a deal that lifts sales but thins margins can help the landlord more than the operator.

lines.text: That tension is why the September 2026 rent relief matters to both sides.
lines.say: That tension is why the September twenty twenty-six rent relief matters to both sides.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: recap.

lines.text: One: in 1956, Harry Sonneborn helped turn McDonald's into a landlord through Franchise Realty Corporation.
lines.say: One. In nineteen fifty-six, Harry Sonneborn helped turn McDonald's into a landlord, through Franchise Realty Corporation.

lines.text: Two: in 2025, rent from franchisees was $10.4 billion, more than all the food sold at McDonald's own restaurants.
lines.say: Two. In twenty twenty-five, rent from franchisees was ten point four billion dollars, more than all the food sold at McDonald's own restaurants.

lines.text: Three: franchise revenue kept about 84 cents on the dollar as margin, versus about 15 cents at its own restaurants.
lines.say: Three. Franchise revenue kept about eighty-four cents on the dollar as margin, versus about fifteen cents at its own restaurants.

lines.text: Four: in September 2026, the landlord offered rent relief to help its tenants upgrade.
lines.say: Four. In September twenty twenty-six, the landlord offered rent relief to help its tenants upgrade.

lines.text: So yes, McDonald's sells burgers. But the burgers are also how the rent gets paid.
lines.say: So yes, McDonald's sells burgers. But the burgers are also how the rent gets paid.

post.ig: In 2025, McDonald's collected $10.4B in rent from franchisees, more than its own restaurants sold. Here's how a burger chain became a landlord.

post.yt_desc:
How McDonald's became a real estate empire. In 2025, McDonald's collected $10.4 billion in rent from franchisees, more than the $9.7 billion of food sold at its own restaurants. This video covers how Ray Kroc and Harry Sonneborn built the landlord model through Franchise Realty Corporation in 1956, where McDonald's $26.9 billion of 2025 revenue came from, a hypothetical rent-and-royalty example ($4 million in sales, 5% royalty, an assumed 10% rent = $600,000), why franchised margins (84.2%) dwarf company-operated margins (14.7%), what McDonald's owns (about 56% of the land and 80% of the buildings in its consolidated markets), and the $8.5 billion franchisee support plan with rent relief announced at its September 23, 2026 Investor Day.
